raw.retained_raw_text: {"schema_version":"chat_response_v1","response_type":"answer","answer_text":"The light-dependent reactions convert light energy into chemical energy stored in energy carriers, which then move to the Calvin cycle. The overall purpose of the light-dependent reactions is to convert light energy into chemical energy, and this chemical energy will be used by the Calvin cycle to fuel the assembly of sugar molecules [ev_008]. Photosystems absorb light and use electron transport chains to convert energy into the chemical energy of ATP and NADPH [ev_002]. The energy carriers that move energy from the light-dependent reactions to the Calvin cycle reactions are thought of as full because they bring energy [ev_001]. These ATP and NADPH molecules travel into the stroma, where the Calvin cycle reactions take place [ev_007]. The Calvin cycle then uses the energy in ATP and NADPH to convert molecules into G3P, and the energy-carrying molecules are used in the fixation and reduction stages that build carbohydrates [ev_010]. After the energy is released, the empty energy carriers return to the light-dependent reactions to obtain more energy [ev_001]. The products ATP and NADPH have very short lifespans, in the range of millionths of seconds, which is why the cell stores their energy in carbohydrates for longer-term use [ev_003].","short_answer":"Light-dependent reactions capture light energy as ATP and NADPH, which carry that energy into the stroma to power the Calvin cycle's assembly of sugars [ev_008] [ev_007].","citations":["ev_001","ev_002","ev_003","ev_007","ev_008","ev_010"],"refusal_reason":null,"follow_up_questions":[],"confidence":0.85,"tutor_question":null,"learner_attempt_evaluation":null}
